14.3. each carried six men, two shield-bearers, two archers stationed on either side; the rest were charioteers, by no means unarmed: for they had several javelins, which, when there was need to fight at close quarters, the reins being let go, they hurled at the enemy.

14.4. But there was scarcely any use of this aid that day. For, as has been said above, the rain, poured more violently than usual, had made the plains slippery and unfit for riding, and the heavy and almost immovable chariots stuck in the mire and quagmires.

14.5. On the other side Alexander, with a free and light column, briskly bore in. The Scythians and Dahae, first of all, assailed the Indians: then he sent Perdiccas with the cavalry against the enemy's right wing.
14.6. Now the battle had stirred on every side, when those who drove the chariots, judging this the last aid of their own people, with loosened reins began to rush into the midst of the hazard.

14.7. That evil was a danger to both. For both the Macedonian foot were trampled at the first onset, and the chariots, driven over slippery and trackless ground, threw off those by whom they were guided.
14.8. The frightened horses of others hurled the cars headlong, not into the quagmires and pools only, but even into the river.

14.9. A few, driven on by the enemy's weapons, penetrated to Porus, who was urging on the fight most fiercely. He, when he saw the chariots scattered and wandering over the whole line without drivers, distributed the elephants to the nearest of his friends.

14.10. Behind them he had placed the foot and the archers and those wont to beat the drums: this stood to the Indians in place of the sound of trumpets, nor were they disturbed by their noise, their ears being long since softened to the familiar sound.
14.11. The image of Hercules was carried before the column of the foot: this was the greatest incentive to the fighters, and to have deserted those who bore it was held a soldier's disgrace.

14.12. They had even sanctioned a capital penalty for those who did not bring it back from the line, the fear which they had once conceived of that enemy being turned even into religious veneration. The Macedonians were checked for a little while by the sight not only of the beasts, but also of the king himself.

14.13. The beasts, set among the armed men, had from afar made the appearance of towers; Porus himself had nearly exceeded human size: the beast on which he rode seemed to add to Porus' size, towering as much above the rest as he himself surpassed other men.
14.14. And so Alexander, having surveyed both the king and the column of the Indians, said: "At last I see a peril matched to my spirit: the business is at once with beasts and with excellent men."

14.15. And, looking at Coenus, he said: "When I, accompanied by Ptolemy and Perdiccas and Hephaestion, make an attack on the enemy's left wing, and you see me in the midst of the heat of the contest, do you move the right and bear your standards against them when they are thrown into confusion. You, Antigenes, and you, Leonnatus, and Tauron, charge now into the middle of the line and press hard upon the front.

14.16. Our spears, exceedingly long and strong, can be of use at no other time more than against the beasts and their drivers: dislodge those who ride them, and stab the beasts themselves. It is a doubtful kind of aid, and rages more fiercely against its own side: for against the enemy it is driven by command, against its own by fear."

14.17. Having spoken these things, he spurred on his horse, the first. And now, as had been determined, he had assailed the ranks of the enemy, when Coenus with a mighty force bore in from the left wing.

14.18. The phalanx too broke through the middle of the Indian line at a single onset. But Porus, where he had perceived the cavalry charging, ordered the beasts to be driven: but the slow and almost immovable animal could not match the swiftness of the horses. Nor was there even any use of arrows to the barbarians.

14.19. For these, long and exceedingly heavy, they do not fit on aptly and conveniently unless they have first set the bow on the ground; then, struggling to make their shots on ground slippery and for that reason hindering the effort, they are forestalled by the speed of the enemy.

14.20. So, the king's command being scorned — which usually happens, when, men being in confusion, fear rather than the commander begins to command — there were as many commanders as there were straying columns:
14.21. one bade them join the line, another divide it; some bade them stand, and not a few ride round the enemy's rear; nothing was decided for the common good.

14.22. Porus, nevertheless, with a few in whom shame had prevailed over fear, set about gathering the scattered, and to go to meet the enemy, and ordered the elephants to be driven before the column of his own men.
14.23. The beasts struck great terror, and their unwonted trumpeting had thrown into confusion not the horses only — an animal so fearful at all things — but men too and their ranks.

14.24. Now those who a little before were victors were looking round for a place of flight, when Alexander sent against the beasts the Agrianians and Thracians, light-armed, soldiers better at skirmishing than in close formation.
14.25. These hurled a vast force of weapons both at the elephants and at those who guided them. The phalanx too began to press steadily on the terrified.
14.26. But some, pursuing the beasts too greedily, provoked them against themselves with wounds.
14.27. Trampled, therefore, under their feet, they were a warning to the rest to press on more sparingly.

14.28. Especially terrible was that sight, when the beasts seized arms and men with their trunks and handed them over their backs to those who guided them. So the doubtful battle, now of those pursuing, now of those fleeing the elephants, drew out the varying contest far into the day, until with axes — for this kind of aid had been prepared — they began to cut off the beasts' feet.

14.29. Copides they called swords slightly curved, like sickles, with which they aimed at the trunks of the beasts. Nor did the fear of death, nor even, in death itself, of a new kind of torment, leave anything untried.

14.30. So the elephants, at last wearied by their wounds, overthrew their own people in their rush, and those who had guided them, hurled to the ground, were trampled by them. And now, like cattle, more frightened than dangerous, they were being driven beyond the line,

14.31. when Porus, deserted by the greater number, began to hurl from his own elephant the many weapons prepared beforehand against those surrounding him. And, many being wounded from afar, he himself, exposed, was aimed at from every side.
14.32. Nine wounds by now he had received, here on the back, there on the breast, and, much blood being shed, with languid hands he threw weapons that slipped rather than were hurled.

14.33. Nor less briskly did the beast, possessed by frenzy, not yet wounded, charge into the ranks, until the beast's driver saw the king, his limbs failing, his arms let go, scarcely master of his mind.
14.34. Then he urged the beast into flight, Alexander pursuing: but his horse, pierced with many wounds and failing, sank, setting down the king rather than throwing him off.

14.35. And so, while he changed his horse, he pursued the more slowly. Meanwhile the brother of Taxiles, the Indian king, sent ahead by Alexander, began to warn Porus not to persist in trying the last extremity, and to surrender to the victor.

14.36. But he, although his strength was exhausted and his blood failing, yet, roused at the familiar voice, said: "I recognize the brother of Taxiles, the betrayer of his own empire and kingdom," and hurled at him the one weapon which by chance had not slipped away: which pierced through the middle of his breast to his back.

14.37. This last work of valour performed, he began to flee more keenly. But the elephant too, which had received many weapons, was failing: so he stayed his flight and set the foot-soldier against the pursuing enemy.

14.38. Now Alexander had come up, and, having learned the obstinacy of Porus, forbade that the resisters be spared. So from every side weapons were heaped both upon the foot and upon Porus himself, by which at last, overborne, he began to slip from the beast.

14.39. The Indian who guided the elephant, judging that he was dismounting, ordered the elephant, after the usual fashion, to kneel down: and when it lowered itself, the rest too — for so they had been trained — sank their bodies to the ground.

14.40. This delivered both Porus and the rest to the victors. The king, believing him killed, ordered the body of Porus to be stripped, and those who should draw off his corslet and garment ran up; when the beast began to defend its master and to attack the spoilers, and, lifting his body up, to set it again upon its back. So it was overwhelmed with weapons on every side, and, it being slain, Porus was placed in a vehicle.

14.41. When the king saw him lifting his eyes, moved not by hatred but by pity, he said: "What madness, in heaven's name, drove you, the fame of my exploits being known, to try the fortune of war, when Taxiles was so near a pattern to you of my clemency toward the surrendered?"

14.42. But he said: "Since you ask, I will answer with the freedom which you have given by asking. I thought no man braver than myself. For I knew my own strength, not yet having tried yours: the outcome of the war has taught me that you are the braver. But not even so am I little fortunate, who am second to you."
14.43. Asked again what he himself judged the victor ought to determine: "What this day," he said, "counsels you, on which you have learned how fleeting good fortune is."

14.44. By his warning he profited more than if he had entreated: for the greatness of his spirit, unterrified and unbroken even by fortune, the king deigned to receive not with compassion only, but even with honour.

14.45. He cared for the sick man no otherwise than if he had fought on his own side: and, when he had recovered, beyond all men's hope, he received him into the number of his friends, and soon presented him with a wider kingdom than he had held.

14.46. Nor indeed did his nature have anything more solid or more constant than admiration of true praise and glory: yet he weighed fame more simply in an enemy than in a fellow-citizen. For he believed that his own greatness could be diminished by his own people, but that the same would be the more illustrious, the greater those had been whom he himself had conquered.
